FORWARD 


The Board of Directors takes pleasure in submitting the Annual 
Report of the Young Men’s Christian Association of Montreal for 
the year, ending December 3ist, 1957, in accordance with the 


requirements of the Constitution. 


This report covers matters of general interest affecting the 

Montreal Association as a whole. Detailed reports of all eleven 
branches, including Sir George Williams College and Schools, have 
been submitted and approved at their respective meetings and are 


included in the records of each brancho

NOMINATING COMMITTEE REPORT 


METROPOLITAN ORGANIZATION 


The Metropolitan organization of the YoMoCeoAcs of Montreal is made 
up of eleven branches, including Sir George Williams College and 
Schools. With the exception of Central and the College, each of 
the branches serves a specific area of Greater Montreal. Central 
Branch and Sir George Williams College and Schools, located in the 
heart of Montreal’s business section, draw their members and 
students from all parts of the city. Each of the Program Branches 
is governed by a Board of Management, while Sir George Williams 


College and Schools is under the direction of a Board of Governorso 


The Metropolitan Board of Directors has general oversight of the 


whole YoMo.CoAo operation in Montrealo 


Central Branch - 1441 Drummond Street - “Drummond-Stanley Building* 
has extensive facilities for physical activities, club rooms, social 
area, food service and a residence which can accommodate 540 meno 
This branch conducted extension units at Strathearn and Devonshire 
Schools in the east downtown area and St. Lambert in 1957. 


NOTE2 30,000 square feet of space in Centrai building is used 
for offices and classrooms by the evening Blementary and 
High Schools, the Business §chool and the School of 
Retailing. The physical and social facilities are also 
used for organized college astivities, as well as indie- 
vidual student useo The Drummond, Stanley and College 
buildings are closely integrated, uging a sentral heat= 
ing plant and a common maintenance staff for purpose of 
economy and efficiencyo

PROGRAM 


Program Modernization - 1957 marks an important point in the program 
modernization of the YoMoCoAo of Montreal. In May, a two-day confere 
ence of the secretarial staff was held at Christieville, at which 
drafts of two documents = “Vales For Living* and a "Guide To Conducting 
Program in the YoMoCoAo of Montreal® = were thoroughly reviewed and 
revised to the point where it was felt they were ready to be put into 


use tentatively. 


The “Values For Living™® suggests the specific purposes, goals and 
objectives of our program, while the “Guide To Conducting Program™ 
states the principles and main methods by which the YoMoCoAo attempts 


to achieve these valueso 


In October, the program committes presented the two documents, at a 
Metropolitan Board meeting they were adopted for experimental use for 
one year, after which they will be revised in terms of experiences 

Plans were completed at the end of the year for a staff training program 
for the purpose of re-orienting staff in understanding and skills for 


putting the principles of these two documents into use in the branches. 


Of the 15 program units, consisting of 11 branches and 4 camps, five 
have accepted the “Values For Living™ as the aims of their program, 
while six have taken preliminary actiono The “Guide To Conducting 


Program® has been acted upon by 9 branches and discussed by 4 otherso 


60 


PROGRAM = continuede 


This whole process has been stimulating to those involved, and encour 


aging results have been evidenced by the growth and development of 


program in the brancheso 


Clubs and Groups 

Opportunities for achieving the “Values For Living” with boys, girls 
and young people are presented when groups of intimate friends are 
related together and participate in activities which are of a whole- 


some naturdo 


These groups are organized on democratic principles and are respons= 


ible for their own programs within the limits of their capacity and 


maturitye Volunteer leaders and counsellors, recruited and trained by 


the YoMcCoAc, help these young people in the operation of their clubs 


In 1954, the Annual Report listed 78 of these clubse.oooo in 1957, there 


were over 500 such groups in the Associatione 


In addition to these, there were a thousand other interest groups and 
classes, making a total of 1,520 with an enrollment of 28,367, and an 


aggregate attendance of 483,436.

Young Adults Camping 


Camp Otorske: This camp provides young adults with an opportunity for 
a Laurentian vacation during June, July and Auguste It is also used 
by many for weekends and holidayso During the year, 1,173 individual 
campers attended the camp a total of 1,577 timeso An informal program 
was planned and run by the campers themselves, which included a large 
variety of social and recreational activities, such as camp fires, 
dances, carnivals, tournaments, all-day outings, overnight canoe trips 
and swimming. Religious services were conducted each Sunday morning 


in an cutdoor Chapelo

Informal Education 

The whole program of the YoMoCoAo of Montreal was conducted in a 
framework of educational processes and methods, with many informal 
activities led by specialists in their various fields. Falling in 
this category were bellet, oil painting, auto mechanics, photography, 
wood working, leathercraft, sewing, smocking, skiing, figure skating, 


archery, pottery making, fencing, and others. 


Total enroliment in these groups was 3,204 different individuals, 
with total attendance of 46,622, while in other areas of informal 
education, such as lectures, forums, study groups and motion pictures, 


there was o total attendance of 49,7760

Swimming Classes = 6,416 individual boys, girls, men and women were 
enrolled in swimming instruction classes during 1957, and 4,755 tests 
were passed successfully. This swimming program consists of a pro- 
gression of tests ranging from the beginner's test through to senior 
life savingo With the frequency of tragic swimming, boating and other 
accidents which could be prevented by a better understanding of swimming, 
its dangers, and what to do in emergencies, the YoMoCoAo considers this 


activity particularly timely and important.

Sir George Williams College And Schools 


Extracurricular Activities; The total program of extracurricular 
activities is extensive and complex. These range from athletics to 
religious clubs and from study groups to the large social events such 
as the Christmas bello Altogether the extracurricular program of the 
College and Schools may well be one of the largest single YoMoCoAo 
branch programs in Canadao The two student societies (the Students? 
Undergraduate Society and the Evening Students’ Association) under 
which activities are conducted have had their own problems with in- 
creased registrationo Nevertheless, nearly all planned events have 
proceeded without undue strain, and the leadership given by student 


officers has in itself been an important aspect of this undertakingo 


Some outstanding aspects of extracurricular activity in 1957 were 

(a) the YoMoC.Ao World Service campaign in which over $3,100 was 
raised, (b) thse freshmen reception week, (c) the Blood Donor 

Clinic with the Canadian Red Cross Society, (d) the World University 
Services display and sale, (6) ‘the Asian Studies group with an exten- 
Sive educational program, (f) the Winter Carnival, (g) the 
“Georgians” (senior basketball) and many other athletic teems, (h) the 
Christmas party, given by the Evening Students’ Association for childe- 
ren of students and the faculty, (i) the Rifle Club, (Jj) Ukranian 


Week, and many otherso

SIR GEORGE WILLIAMS COLLEGE AND SCHOOL 


The academic year, 1956-57, marked the first full year of operation 
in the new building, and the end of 1957 saw it used to almost som-= 
plete capacity. Thus a plan of development expected to take three 


years was completed in a year and a half'o 


After long consideration, the Board of Governors announced in February 
that an engineering course in both day and evening divisions would open 
in the Fall, with a limited registration of thirty students in each 


division for the inaugural yearo 


Convocations 

During 1957, three convocations were heldo The first on February 23rd 
for the purpose of installing Dro Ho Fe Hall as Principale The regular 
Spring Convocation took place on May 24th at St. James United Church, 
and a Fall Convocation was held on November 23rd in Birks Hall. The 
Business College, School of Art, School of Retailing, and Evening 
Elementary and High Schools all held separate graduation exercises. 


In all, 408 degrees and 411] Giplomas and certificates were awarded.

Sir George Williams College and Schools has been accurately referred 
to as the "College of the Second Chance,” because it provides through 
evening classes an opportunity for further education for students 
holding full-time jobs and working during the dayo By far the larger 
number of students attend the evening division: 854% of the total 
registratione 183 firms of the Montreal area have five or more of 
their personnel enrolled in the student bodyo Many nationalities are 
represented at the Colleges In all, students of 47 different mother= 


tongues are enrollede

PERSONAL SERVICES 


The emphasis of the Yo.Mo.C.Ao since its inception has been on the value 
of individual personality, and while it is impossible to measure acce- 
urately the effect of the YoM.C.A.o on the lives of individuals, mention 


is made here of two of the more tangible personal services. 


In The Men’s Residenses 
Three of our branches, Central, International and Westmount, have men’s 


residences which provide accommodation at a reasonable cost to young 


meno During 1957, this service supplied 191,213 bed nightso 


The residence of the Central Branch, located in the downtown area, 
attracts the student, the serviceman, the “Y® member from another city 
or another country, the foreign visitor, or the young man coming to 
the city for the first timeo While in Montreal they are rendered many 
of the services needed to make their stay in our city as pleasant and 


wholesome as possible. 


Personal Interviews and Counselling 


Sir George Williams College maintains a counselling service which 
emphasizes personal adjustment through psychological testing and 
counselling, to establish realistic educational and vocational goals 
for each studento The College also maintains office space for two 
full time Placement Officers through cooperation with the National 


Employment Services 


186 


PERSONAL SERVICES = continuede 


Many people wishing to do so find an opportunity to talk over their 
problems with an understanding person at any of the “Y* branches. 


In 1957, 69,108 persons availed themselves of this service, while 


587 were helped by the Y.MeCoAo to locats jobse

EMPHASIS 


“The YoMoCoAc is a world-wide fellowship of men and boys united by a 
common loyalty to Jesus Christ for the purpose of developing Christian 
personality and building a Christian society” -- these familiar words, 
known as the YoMoCoAo purpose as stated by the International Cleveland 
Convention, 1931, continue to be the fundamental basis of all the work 
of the Montreal Y.MoC.Aco Reference has been made in the program sec= 
tion about the steps which are being taken to express our basic purpose 
in a workable framework, entitled "Values for Living.” This study and 
examination of methods and tools and the modus operandi of the program 
dosa not detract or eliminate in any way much that has been done in 
the past but makes possible a more significant performance in the real- 


ization of goalso 


To delineate the extent to which basic purposes are being realized is 
a task which would defy the wisdom of a Solomon, and yet it is def- 
initely known that day by day, the impact on hundreds of lives as the 
program is adding its contribution toward the development of Christian 
personality. Christian emphasis to some is related to certain acti- 
vities = to those however on whom the planning and execution of the 
YoMoCoAc programs rests it is not omly specific activities but a plus 
factor permeating all = a motivating forse behind the entire range of 
activities which leaves its imprint, sometimes readily discernable, at 


other times in a manner which may not be found in overt expressione 


200 


EMPHASIS = continued. 


Formal worship services, devotional periods, induction services, 
religious discussions, camp fire services, personal interviews, 
Conferences, circulation of Week of Prayer booklets, are typical 

of the kinds of activity where direct Christian emphasis is an 
integral part of the programo “The Captain’s Chapel” in the Central 


Building has been open daily for meditation. 


2lo 


MEMORIALS COMMITTEE 


This is a standing committee of the Board of Directors. It was est= 
ablished several years ago under the chairmanship of Mro George Hodge 
to arrange for proper recognition of former officers and leaders of 
the Associations Under its direction, bronze plaques were erected in 
the Central Branch foyer, recognizing the service of former members 
of the Montreal YoM.oC.A.o in two World Wars; names of early leaders 
have been inscribed in the Hall of Remembrance leading to the 
Captain's Chapels and plates have been installed in certain rooms 

in Central Branch and the Collegs Building, recognizing special meme= 


orial donations of rooms and equipment. 


During the last year, the attention of the Committee has been given 

to gathering significant data and material for the Book of Remembranse, 
and to deciding on the most svitable means of inscribing it in the 
booke Progress has been made in this endeavour and it is hoped that 


this work will be completed shortlyo

CITY-WIDE COOPERATION 


A close relationship was maintained with many community groups and 


organizations, and facilities were made available to 1,279 community 
groups a total of 2,770 times. 


As a member of the Greater Montreal Council of Churches, the Counsil 
of Christian Education for the Provinse of Quebec, and the Montreal 
Council of Social Agencies, the YoMoCoAo continued to assume a helpful 


role in the activities of these organizationse 


Three of the branch buildings were used during the year for worship 


services by religious groups having no buildings of their ownoe 


With greater emphasis on decentralized program, increasing use was 
made of school facilities for its various activities. These schools 


supplement the facilities of branch buildings.e 


The success of the "Learn-to-Swim® campaign was due in no small measure 


to the cooperation received from the schools. 


Cooperation with parents and the home is an integral part of the pro- 
gramo With the knowledge that personal maturity depends upon estab- 
lishing easy working relationships with adults at an early age, increas- 
ing attention is being given to the value of involving parents and 
children in program togethero This is done by conducting family swims, 
outings, parents’ nights, father-son and mother-daughter programso Par- 
ents also have demonstrated their interest by working on committees, 
councils, boards, and as advisors and instructors in clubs and recreation= 


al activitiseso

FINANCE AUD PROPERT 


The Financial Campsign, the largest single annual undertaking organized 
on a Metropolitan basis, was hald November 18th to December 2nd with an 
ob jective of $225,000. The experience and results were excellent in 
spite of substantial losses, though deaths, removals, eteo The organi- 
zational structure was strong, the leadership effective, the morale of 
workers good, and the pre-campaign efforts to inform, to enthuse, and 
to guide workers reached a larger number than usualo The final returns 


showed $233,000 having been secured from 13,812 contributors. 


Mro Wo So Kirkpatrick for the second time as General Chairman, gave 
excellent leadership to the undertakings Mre Lo Ho Te Clegg, as Chairs 
man of Special Names, assumed the responsibility of this important role 
most effectivelys Mro Re Eo Heartz was Vice-Chairman of Special Nameso 
The Sponsors’ list numbered 218, including 7 new nameso In addition, 

15 laymen rendered excellent service as Chairmen of Divisions. It 
should be noted that the Lakeshore Division related to the “baby bransch® 
emerged as an effective canvassing organization, doing a comprehensive 
coverage of the district. The publicity program was again under the 
able direction of Mro Jack Clifford. The opening meeting was unique 

in that it was addressed by a member of the Metropolitan Board, Dro Ho Ho 
Lank, President of DuPont Company of Canada Limited. Dro Lank called 
attention to the significant role of the YoMoCoAo in the contemporary 


scene and commended the effort about to be undertekeno The usual report

During the year the Association sold 98,585 sqoft. of land from the 
Southwestern Branch holdings to the Catholic School Commission of Verduno 
The decision to release this property was based on the fact that the 
Association’s constituency is becoming further removed from the present 


building and relocation at some future date is inevitable. 


At the year end, a further offer to buy the remaining land and building 
was under consideration and steps were being taken to negotiate the sale 


at the most favorable prises

PERSONNEL 


As the YoMoCoA. of Montreal continued to expand into new areas in 1957, 
a larger number of persons became invelved in its worko Many acted on 
boards and committees, others gave volunteer leadership in program as 
advisors and sounsellors, while many employed personnel were required 
for building and equipment maintenance, clerical work, food and resi- 
ence services, instruction in College and Schools, and to work with 
committees and volunteers in the administration and program of the 


Associationo 


Boards and Committees 

The affairs of the Association were administered by the Metropolitan 
Board of Directors, Branch Boards of Management, and committees related 
to the various departments and sections of its worko During the year, 


2,705 persons were active on boards and committeeso 


Volunteer Leaders 

Many thousands of hours of volunteer leadership were given by people 
who acted as advisors, leaders, instructors and counsellors in many 
crafts, interest groups, clubs and camping programso The total number 


of 1,823 people were involved in this wey during 1957. 


Staff 
During the year there were 3350 full-time employees, while 575 were 


employed on a part<time basis. Included in the part-time personnel

NATIONAL COUNCIL 


This Association played host to the Annual Meeting of the National 


Council of YoMoCeoAos of Canada in February of 1957 when representa] 


tives from all parts of the Country and National Council staff members 


visited Montreal. 


The meeting, held in the renovated facilities of the Drummond-Stanley 


Building, was a successful one due, in no small measure, to the adapt- 


ability of the accommodation and the cooperation of a local planning 


Gommitteeo One of the sessions involved attendance at the inaugura] 


tion of Dro Ho Fe Hall as Principal of Sir George Williams College, 


thus relating this important institution to the YoMoCoAo nationally 


in an important wayo 


In addition to the Annual Meeting, Montreal continued to play an active 


part in this national body, and the following members of the YoMoCoAo 


of Montreal were members of the National Council of YoMcoCoA-s of Canada:

World Services ig a special and much valued part of our Association 
work. For while it is well-known that youth has been, and is, the 
central and primary concern of the YoMoCoAo = their physical well- 
being, their strength of mind and above all their Christian character - 
it is not so well-known that to us the term “Youth” means the youth 


of the world. 


For sixty-nine yearge World Services has been a joint program of the 
YoMcoCoAo’s of the United States and Canada which has brought the “y® 
to 42 of the 76 sountries where the Association now operates. In that 
time an estimated thirteen million of the world’s youth have been act= 
ive members, while millions more have been helped by boys’ clubs, 
schools, sanitation drives, physical education, rural reconstruction, 


ato 


Ideas = as well as missiles ~ need proving grounds, and in many countries 
the YoMoCoAo provides the only opportunity for young people to see demo~ 
cracy in action, under the guidance of one of 56 skilled North American 
“Y" Secretaries. These Canadians and Americans form the apex of a 
pyramid of workers = 30 paid and 350 unpaid native leaders are serving 
for each fraternal secretary overseas. In this way it has been poss- 
ible to develop across the world a series of Associations which have 
learned self-reliance, growth and adjustment to the changing conditions 


of today in the formsr colonial continents. 


35 0 


WORLD SERVICE &§ = continuedo 


From its inception in 1889, this extraordinary international service 
has been an integral part of the Montreal Association, with untold 
spiritual benefits accruing as a result of this concern for other 
people in distant lands. The number of friends who support this 
undertaking are steadily increasing. During the year we were fortun- 
ate to have first-hand accounts from two overseas speakers about the 
work; Quentin Gallagher, an American from the Egyptian “Y" organiz- 
ation; and Barle Buckley, a Canadian on the National “Y* staff of 


JAPano 


In 1957, World Services raised a total of $1,501,444.003 Canada’s 


total was $142,268.00. Our local results were as follows;

WORLD’? § ALLIANCE 


The World’s Alliance of YoM.CoA's. is the name given to the network 
of more than 10,000 senters in 76 countries and territories around 

the earth, where the ideals and ideas of the “Y® are at worke In 
organization, the Alliance is a federation of national movements of 
YoMoCoAts., for example the National Council of YoMoCoA®s. of Canada 
is one national movement which belongs: in other cases, several 
countries may be in one movement, as with the South American which has 
sight nations, or the British with England, Wales and Ireland. (The 


Scottish have a separate National Councils) 


This Alliance, with headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, has been 
steadily growing since six countries sent a total of 99 young men as 
representatives to the first international conference of YoMoCoA’s. in 
Paris in 1855. Since then, despite wars, revolutions, economic up-= 
heavals and latterly, atomic age tensions, the “Y" has steadily ex- 
tended its world-wide coverages and has become a strong force for world 
brotherhoods The Alliance enables the Association to keep open reg-= 
ular global channels for the exchange of ideas and techniques and for 
the training of personnel. It also enables the Association to speak 
with one voice at international levels in the realms of government, 
education and the United Nations. Approximately five percent of World 


Service receipts are allocated for the support of the Alliances 


The official publication of the Alliance, called World Communique, is 


350 


WORLD* § ALLIANCE = continued. 


well-known in Montreal. For several years 500 copies quarterly have 
been coming to homes in this city. It is an outstanding example of 
an attractive periodical presenting a Christian viewpoint in a stimu- 


lating and interesting mannero

OBITUARY 


We record with sorrow the passing of a number of friends of the 


Association = 


Walter Po Zeller, a member of the Advisory Board, was Chairman of the 
Maintenance Campaign for two successive years and served on the Metro-= 


politan Board and Advisory Board for a period of fourteen yearso 


Dro Kenneth E. Norris, Principal Emeritus of Sir George Williams 
Collegeo Until retirement because of ill health in 1956, Dro Norris 
served the Y.MoCoAo in Ottawa and Montreal for thirty-two yearso He 
joined the staff of Sir George Williams College in 1929 and became 
principal in 19360 He gave outstanding leadership to the College 
during a period of phenomenal growth, involving incorporation as a 


university and erection of a new buildings 


Dro Norris also made a significant contribution to the YoMoC.Ao in 

the local, national and international fields through his association 
with research, personnel, and professional education activitieso But 

for ill health, he would have been elested to the Presidency of the 
Association of Secretaries, the highest honor to be accorded any YoMoCoAo 


secretary in North America 


Outstanding educator, valued YoMoCoAo secretary, warm, personal friend, 


Dro Norris left a gap in the professional ranks of the Association,

1957 was a good year for the Montreal Young Men’s Christian Associations 
Many important aspects of the Association's life have recorded satis- 
factory gains: the program modernization project has continued to move 
forward; the number of volunteer leaders has increased; the number 

of self-directing club-groups and the program attendance have reached 
new highs; the College and Schools enrolment has made impressive gains; 
and the financial position of the Association has shown improvement 
These and much else that has been dealt with in the body of the report 


have engendered a sense of progreas and forward-snoveo 


Progress has not only been in the direction of more and better astiv- 
ities but also in the manner in which the Association has continued to 
adapt its program and organization to the social and economic changes 


that are taking place at a greatly accelerated paceo 


The very precious and essential quality that provides vitality and 
forward-push to the Association is the sincere and unreserved dedisa= 
tion of the leadership; Board and Committeemen, secretarial personnel 
and voluntary leaders, to the Christian purposes of the movement.o This 
very sincere desire to personally find and practice the Christian way 
of life and to encourage and assist others in this life-quest is the 
motivating force behind the direction given by responsible leaders of 


the YoMoCoAo 


41 


CONCLUSION @=]= continued. 


We are grateful for the confidence in the Association that members, 
parents and friends and community leaders have indicated in many wayso 
Our goals and purposes being what they are, our task and our aspirations 
are never-endingo The accomplishments and gains herein reported are 
many and of solid substance and provide encouragement and incentive as 
we continue to bend our best efforts toward preserving and strengthening 


a society of free people motivated by Christian principles. 


Respectfully submitted, 


———————— 


Fred Go Hubbard, 
General Secretary.

April 15, 1958. 


The Young Men’s Christian Association of Montreal. 
Montreal, Quebeco 


We have examined the Balance Sheet of The Young Men's Christian 
Association of Montreal as at December 31, 1957, and the related 
Statement cf Income and Expenditures for the year ended that date. 
In connection therewith we made a test examination of the books of 
account and financial records of the Metropolitan Office and of 
the reports from the branches and from the Residence Building but 
we did not make a detailed audit of the transactions of the 
Association for the yearo We have received all the information 


and explanations we have required. 


In our opinion, based on the examination made, ths attached Balance 
Sheet and related Statement of Income and Expenditures correctly set 
forth the financial position of the Association as at December 31, 1957, 
and the results of its operations for the year ended on that date, 
according to the best of our information and the explanations given 


to us and as shown by the accounting records examined by use 


Pe Se ROSS & SONS. 


Chartered Acsountanto

NOMINATING COMMITTEE 


The Report of the Nomi nating Committee to the Annual Meeting 


of the Young Men’s Christian Association of Montreal 


Monday, April 21st, 1958 


Mr. President 
Your Committee, having carried out its duties in accordance with the 
Constitution, hereby nominates the following active members to become 


Direstors of the Associations 


DoSo Abbott 
EoRo Alexander 
RoDo Armstrong 
JodoFo Bancroft 
Ao Turner Bone 
LoHoTo Clegg 
AoHo Cowie 


Ho Roy Crabtree 
JoRo Crawford 
Go Arnold Hart 
To Denton Lewis 
HoMo Mawhinney 
S.Co Norsworthy 
AoEo Sargent 


Your Committee also wishes to report that at the last meeting of the 
Metropolitan Board of Directors, the following were elected members 


of the Advisory Boards 


Henry Go Birks Hod. Hannaford AoCo Jensen 
JoHo Davey RoDo Harkness Fo Johnson 
CoAo Dunning GoRo Hodgson AoLo Paterson 


BoC. Gardner RoC. Holden DoAo Whittaker 


Respectfully submitted, 


RoE. Heartg, Chairman 
JoDo McKeown 

I oRo Tait 

Frank Adams
